title: Curvature of the derived background

key_results.statement: For fixed $\lambda$, $x$ and $v$, $\alpha(x,x+\varepsilon v;\lambda)^2=\varepsilon^2 g_{ab}(x;\lambda)v^av^b+O(\varepsilon^3)$ as $\varepsilon\to0$, hence $\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\alpha/\varepsilon=\sqrt{g_{ab}v^av^b}$: the background metric $g$ is the infinitesimal form of the witness angle, and by polarization $\alpha$ determines $g$.

Exact for $\lambda>0$, entire in $\lambda$ and jointly smooth in $(x,\lambda)$: $\hat g_{ab}(x;\lambda)=\operatorname{Cov}_\chi(\bar K_a,\bar K_b)$ (symmetrized covariance in $\chi$), with $\bar K_a=\frac1\lambda\int_0^\lambda e^{\mathrm{i}Ms}K_ae^{-\mathrm{i}Ms}\,\mathrm{d}s$, $M=K+B$ and $K_a=\partial_aK$.
If $[M(x),K_a(x)]=0$ for all $a$, then $\bar K_a=K_a$ and $\hat g_{ab}(x;\lambda)=\operatorname{Cov}_\chi(K_a,K_b)$ for every $\lambda$.

$\hat g^{(0)}_{ab}(x)=\operatorname{Cov}_\chi(K_a,K_b)=g(\partial_au,\partial_bu)$, i.e. $\hat g^{(0)}=u^*g$ is the pullback of the Euclidean metric $g(v,w)=\operatorname{Re}\langle v\vert w\rangle$ of $\mathcal{H}_c$ by the record map $u$; $\hat g^{(0)}(v,v)=\operatorname{Var}_\chi(v^aK_a)$, and $\hat g^{(0)}(x)$ is non-degenerate iff $u$ is an immersion at $x$.

Body-free part of the first-order term (expectations in $\chi$, all operators at $x$): $\hat g^{(1,0)}_{ab}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{4}\langle[K,\{\tilde K_a,\tilde K_b\}]\rangle=-\frac12\operatorname{Im}\langle K\{\tilde K_a,\tilde K_b\}\rangle$; it is all of $\hat g^{(1)}$ when $B=0$.

Body part of the first-order term, linear in $B$: $\hat g^{(1,B)}_{ab}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{4}\langle[B,\{\tilde K_a,\tilde K_b\}]\rangle=-\frac12\operatorname{Im}\langle B\{\tilde K_a,\tilde K_b\}\rangle$; so $\hat g^{(1)}=\hat g^{(1,0)}+\hat g^{(1,B)}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{4}\langle[K+B,\{\tilde K_a,\tilde K_b\}]\rangle$.

For $x_h=x$, $x_{h'}=x+\varepsilon v$ and $D=K_h-K_{h'}$ the coefficients of (6.9)–(6.11) reduce to the metric components: $\operatorname{Var}_\chi(D)=\varepsilon^2\hat g^{(0)}(v,v)+O(\varepsilon^3)$, $c_3^{(0)}=-\varepsilon^2\hat g^{(1,0)}(v,v)+O(\varepsilon^3)$ and $\operatorname{Im}\langle B\tilde D^2\rangle=-\varepsilon^2\hat g^{(1,B)}(v,v)+O(\varepsilon^3)$; so $\hat g^{(0)}$ is the infinitesimal form of $d_0$ in (5.10) and $-\hat g^{(1)}$ that of $c_3^{(\beta_0)}$, part by part.

Tangent and normal parts of the second derivatives of the record map: $\partial_a\partial_bu=\Gamma^p_{ab}\,\partial_pu+\mathrm{II}_{ab}$ with $g(\mathrm{II}_{ab},\partial_mu)=0$, where $\Gamma^p_{ab}$ are the Levi-Civita symbols of $\hat g^{(0)}$ and $\mathrm{II}_{ab}$ is the second fundamental form of the record surface $u(U)\subset(\mathcal{H}_c,g)$.

Gauss equation, where $\hat g^{(0)}$ is non-degenerate: $\hat R^{(0)}_{abmn}=g(\mathrm{II}_{am},\mathrm{II}_{bn})-g(\mathrm{II}_{an},\mathrm{II}_{bm})=g(\partial_a\partial_mu,\partial_b\partial_nu)-g(\partial_a\partial_nu,\partial_b\partial_mu)-\hat g^{(0)pq}(\Gamma_{am|p}\Gamma_{bn|q}-\Gamma_{an|p}\Gamma_{bm|q})$, with $\Gamma_{ab|m}=g(\partial_a\partial_bu,\partial_mu)$.

For $k=2$, where $\hat g^{(0)}$ is non-degenerate, the Gaussian curvature of $\hat g^{(0)}$ is $\kappa^{(0)}=\frac{g(\mathrm{II}_{11},\mathrm{II}_{22})-g(\mathrm{II}_{12},\mathrm{II}_{12})}{\hat g^{(0)}_{11}\hat g^{(0)}_{22}-(\hat g^{(0)}_{12})^2}$.

Sufficient condition for flatness of $\hat g^{(0)}$: if $\mathrm{II}\equiv0$, i.e. $\partial_a\partial_bu(x)\in\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{\partial_1u(x),\dots,\partial_ku(x)\}$ for all $x,a,b$, then $\hat R^{(0)}\equiv0$. It holds for affine $K$, for $k=2(d_c-1)$ and for $k=1$.

$\hat g^{(0)}$, $\mathrm{II}$ and $\hat R^{(0)}$ are the same with and without a body, for every $B$, and depend on $\chi$ only through covariances: $\hat g^{(0)}_{ab}=\operatorname{Cov}_\chi(K_a,K_b)$, $\Gamma_{ab|m}=\operatorname{Cov}_\chi(K_{ab},K_m)$, $g(\partial_a\partial_mu,\partial_b\partial_nu)=\operatorname{Cov}_\chi(K_{am},K_{bn})$, with $K_{ab}=\partial_a\partial_bK$.

For $k=2$ and non-degenerate $\hat g^{(0)}$: $\hat\kappa(x;\lambda)=\kappa^{(0)}+\lambda\,\dot\kappa[\hat g^{(1)}]+O(\lambda^2)$, where the first variation of the Gaussian curvature is $\dot\kappa[h]= rac12 igl(

For $k=2$, the body changes the Gaussian curvature of $\hat g$ at order $\lambda$: $\hat\kappa|_B-\hat\kappa|_{B=0}=\lambda\,\dot\kappa[\hat g^{(1,B)}]+O(\lambda^2)$ with $\hat g^{(1,B)}_{ab}=-\frac12\operatorname{Im}\langle\chi\vert B\{\tilde K_a,\tilde K_b\}\vert\chi\rangle$; for $g$ the change is $\lambda^{-1}\dot\kappa[\hat g^{(1,B)}]+O(1)$.

The body-induced change vanishes, $\hat\kappa|_B-\hat\kappa|_{B=0}=O(\lambda^2)$, if (V1) $\hat g^{(1,B)}\equiv0$, which holds when $B\chi=\beta\chi$, or $[B,K_a(x)]=0$ for all $a,x$, or $\{\tilde K_a,\tilde K_b\}\chi=z_{ab}\chi$ for all $a,b,x$; or (V2) $K$ is affine; or (V3) $\hat g^{(1,B)}=\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g^{(0)}$ for a vector field $\xi$ with $\xi^a\partial_a\kappa^{(0)}=0$.

Qubit plane without a body ($K=x\sigma_x+y\sigma_y$, $\chi=\vert0\rangle$), exact, in polar label coordinates $(x,y)=r(\cos\phi,\sin\phi)$: $g=\lambda^2\mathrm{d}r^2+\frac14\sin^2(2\lambda r)\,\mathrm{d}\phi^2$, with $g_{ab}=\lambda^2\delta_{ab}$ at $r=0$; $g$ is non-degenerate except on the circles $r=m\pi/(2\lambda)$, $m=1,2,\dots$.

Qubit plane: $\hat\kappa=4\lambda^2$ and $\kappa_g=4$ wherever $g$ is non-degenerate, for every $\lambda>0$; with a body of arbitrary self-adjoint $B$ on $\mathbb{C}^2$ the Gaussian curvature of $g$ does not change (it is again $4$ where $g$ is non-degenerate).

Commuting plane without a body ($K=x\sigma_x^{(1)}+y\sigma_x^{(2)}$, $\chi=\vert00\rangle$), exact: $g=\lambda^2(\mathrm{d}x^2+\mathrm{d}y^2)$, $\hat g=\mathrm{d}x^2+\mathrm{d}y^2$ and $\kappa_g=\hat\kappa=0$ for every $\lambda$; the metric is non-degenerate everywhere.

Curved record map on $\mathbb{C}^3$: the record map $u$ is a round sphere of radius $R$ in $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{e_2,e_3,\mathrm{i}e_2\}$, so $\hat g^{(0)}=R^2(\mathrm{d}\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\varphi^2)$ and $\kappa^{(0)}=R^{-2}$.

Curved record map: $\{\tilde K_a,\tilde K_b\}\chi=2\hat g^{(0)}_{ab}\chi$, hence $\hat g^{(1,B)}=0$ for every self-adjoint $B$ on $\mathbb{C}^3$ and also $\hat g^{(1,0)}=0$; so $\hat g=\hat g^{(0)}+O(\lambda^2)$ and $\hat\kappa=R^{-2}+O(\lambda^2)$ for every $B$.

open_issues: The order-λ² terms of ĝ and κ̂ are not computed. In 4(a) and 4(c) the body affects κ̂ at most at order λ²; in 4(a) it has no effect at all. No example with a nonzero first-order body-induced curvature is exhibited; such an example needs a non-affine K, a medium of dimension at least 3, and violation of (V1)–(V3).
The conditions (V1)–(V3) and (19.11) are sufficient, not necessary.
Global questions are not addressed: the degeneracy sets (for example the circles in 4(a)), and the relation between the geodesic distance of g and α.

consistency_checks.check: Scaling and dimensions: under (K,B)→(sK,sB), ψ_x(λ)→ψ_x(sλ) and ĝ(λ)→s²ĝ(sλ), which requires ĝ⁽⁰⁾→s²ĝ⁽⁰⁾ and ĝ⁽¹⁾→s³ĝ⁽¹⁾; (19.4) is quadratic and (19.5)–(19.6) are cubic in (K,B), as required. In (19.10) II scales as s and det ĝ⁽⁰⁾ as s⁴, so κ⁽⁰⁾ scales as s⁻², matching R→sR in (19.19); κ_g=4 in 4(a) is scale-invariant; λK is dimensionless, so ĝ⁽⁰⁾ and λĝ⁽¹⁾ carry the same dimension [K]².

Special cases: for k=1, (19.9) vanishes by antisymmetry, as every 1-dimensional metric must; for B equal to a multiple of the identity the body only adds a global phase to ψ_x, and consistently (19.6) gives ĝ^(1,B)=0.

Exact versus perturbative (4a): expanding (19.16) gives ĝ=δ+O(λ²); this matches (19.4), since the covariance of σ_a and σ_b in |0⟩ is δ_ab, and (19.5), which vanishes because {σ_a,σ_b}=2δ_ab; correspondingly κ̂=4λ² has no terms of order 1 or λ, in line with (19.11) and (19.15).
